name: Marco Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Marco, 58, an experienced mid-level developer at a tech company that maintains cemetery plot records. I have a bachelor's degree and a good wage, but I still check old map grids with the registrar before changing a family's record. I have never used AI tools. My partner manages a community kitchen, our daughters are grown, and our home is paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the cemetery office that a plot number must match the paper map before a family is sent to it. I maintain burial-record software for a tech company and have never used AI; I compare a changed record with the registrar's signed ledger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI does little, my experienced mid-level job and our household pay should remain steady. My developer wage is high, my partner is a full-time community kitchen manager, we paid off our home, and we have eleven months of expenses saved, with other software firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep correcting plot-number errors against the bound ledger and teach the new junior how the old map grid is numbered during our normal paid handover. We'd save 130 more monthly while both wages hold, because I have not checked retirement statements yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our bills. I still think a family deserves directions to the right grave on the first visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you find the swapped plots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two adjoining plots had been swapped when an old map was scanned. The registrar opened the bound ledger, and I corrected the cemetery's digital plot record before the family came to leave flowers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughters fund retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown daughters have their own homes. They know where the family graves are, but their wages are not part of our retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI could write records code and answer a family's location question, but the old plot map should decide which name belongs where. I would not want an automatic reply to send mourners to the wrong row.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My experienced role might last longer than a junior's, but routine corrections could still leave fewer hours for me. Eleven months saved helps, yet losing the larger wage would change how soon we can stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a list of swapped-map corrections and bring it to the registrar's scheduled review. I'd ask the manager to publish the staffing plan and to keep a paid person responsible for checking the bound ledger; my partner and I would defer replacing our old car until those hours are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours, though the bills are covered for now. I am slow to trust a new tool because a wrong grave location is difficult to undo in a family's memory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the cropped map hide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bound map uses letters on one edge and numbers on the other. A scanned image was cropped by one column; the ledger showed why the digital plot had the wrong family name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can the car wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our car still starts and passes its checks. We can wait a year rather than spend cash while my paid hours are uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 might write cemetery code before groundskeeping robots arrive around 2031. A family should still have someone to ask when a screen points to the wrong grave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could cut my post once it trusts cheaper code. My partner's kitchen wage covers basic bills, but not every health and travel cost; eleven months saved is search time, not a pension amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd check four nearby software firms and the cemetery office for actual paid records, mapping or support vacancies and written wages. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed role whose pay with my partner's covers utilities, food, health and travel; if none qualifies, I'd seek other available paid local work using savings and check health-cover dates before a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing a job I still need, even with our home paid off. A family needing the right plot does not mean the office has a paid desk for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you show another employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show another employer the cropped-map correction without a family's names. The ledger and map grid explain why the digital record was wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which offer terms matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would compare start date and paid hours with the kitchen rota. If a new role leaves us without health cover for weeks, a higher annual figure would not make it safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives time to hand over the old plot-grid rules before thinking AI reaches the code. Groundskeeping robots follow around 2034, but the record error arrives on a screen first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might remain useful if the firm pays me to maintain a checked archive and teach the next worker. I will not treat being called an 'elder expert' as an income unless paid hours and authority are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep comparing changed plot numbers with the bound map and ask my manager for approved paid time to teach a junior the cropped-column case. If the firm offers a written archive-maintainer post with authority to correct records and wages with my partner's covering utilities, food, health and travel, I'd accept it after 2031; otherwise I'd keep paid coding while offered and seek actual paid local records work if cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about whether the firm will pay for the handover, but I can ask for a proper rota. I would rather leave a usable ledger than a speech about my experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the handover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the cropped scan, the original letter-number grid and the corrected plot side by side in the training file, with family names removed. The junior should be able to find the missing column without me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner need in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner wants the archive role's hours and health cover in writing. We will not replace a good wage with an honorary title because it sounds respectful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 might take me to 68, but thinking AI will still reach cemetery records before groundskeeping robots around 2039. A bound ledger can outlast the software without earning anyone's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Today our two wages, paid-off home and eleven-month reserve feel secure. I have not checked any pension amount, and I cannot assume a future archive job will still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the plot-grid handover current and save 130 monthly while both wages hold, then request both retirement statements and compare verified amounts with utilities, food, health and travel. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if those figures cover bills; otherwise I'd keep a paid role if offered or seek actual local work without counting our daughters' wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant work picture, but current bills are covered. I want family records kept straight even if I am no longer the one writing the fixes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you leave for the registrar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The handover would show the cropped scan and original grid without names. I would ask the registrar to keep the paper map available when software disagrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would daughters cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughters know the stories behind family graves, not the amount of my future pension. They should not be asked to fill in a number I have not checked.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because records code could lose its paid value before another employer offers a real post. Written cut timing, actual records vacancies and uninterrupted health cover would help us use savings responsibly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a family should trust the digital map more than the bound one. A family can read a stone in the ground; the record must lead them to the correct stone.

headlineQuote: A family can read a stone in the ground; the record must lead them to the correct stone.
portrait: Marco, **58**, is an experienced mid-level cemetery-record developer with a bachelor's degree who checks plot changes against bound maps.
His **higher wage**, partner's kitchen pay, paid-off home, eleven-month reserve and many nearby firms secure present bills.
He has **never used AI** and teaches a junior the old grid only with manager-approved paid time.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** him; a new archive role needs written correction authority, wages and uninterrupted health cover.
He keeps **paper maps** available for family disputes and verifies retirement income before leaving paid work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his records wage before a qualifying local paid post appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut timing**, real records vacancies and uninterrupted health cover would help.
